findings.title: Remove build-time `curl | sh` of unpinned script from reserved placeholder domain
findings.whyItBreaks: The added layer executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh returns as root during image build with no pinning, checksum, or vendor verification — a textbook supply-chain RCE sink: any control of the transport or hostname yields arbitrary code in the image. Independently, it cannot legitimately work: example.com is an IANA-reserved documentation domain (RFC 2606) that serves an HTML page, not an installer, so a successful fetch pipes HTML into `sh` (build fails parsing it), and nothing in the repo consumes whatever it was meant to install (rg over the tree shows no other reference; `curl` is already provided by apk on line 2). The step must not merge in either reading.

findings.title: Fetch failure silently swallowed: pipe exit status makes empty install succeed
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker RUN uses `/bin/sh -c`, so the layer's exit status is the pipeline's last command (`sh`), not `curl`; `-s` additionally suppresses error output and there is no `--fail`. On transport failure (offline builder, DNS failure, TLS error) curl writes nothing and exits non-zero, `sh` reads empty stdin and exits 0, and the layer is committed as successful with nothing installed. The failure signal never reaches the build: subsequent layers (COPY, CMD, push) proceed on the false success, and failure is indistinguishable from success at the only decision point (layer exit status).

findings.title: Remove unverified `curl | sh` of remote script from image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh returns in a root shell during docker build, with no version pin, checksum, or signature — any compromise, hijack, or redirect of that host (or DNS path) runs arbitrary code at build time and the result is baked into the published image layer. Supply-chain review class: downloaded artifact executed without verification. Compounding it, `-sL` without `--fail` means an HTTP error (404/5xx) does not stop the step — the error page body is piped into sh anyway — and the pipeline exit status is sh's, so curl's non-zero exit on network failure is discarded (no pipefail); a failed/empty download can make the RUN exit 0 'successfully', shipping an image silently missing whatever this step was supposed to install.

findings.title: Remove unverified `curl | sh` of example.com/install.sh from build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added line pipes https://example.com/install.sh straight into `sh` during image build. example.com is the IANA reserved documentation domain; /install.sh returns a 404 HTML page, and because `curl -sL` lacks `--fail`, curl exits 0 and feeds the HTML body to `sh`, which fails to parse it -> RUN exits non-zero -> `docker build` aborts, so the image cannot be produced at all. Worse, the pattern itself is a supply-chain defect: whatever the URL serves executes as root inside the build with no pinning, checksum, or signature verification, so any repoint/compromise of the URL silently injects code into the image. There is no vendor, version, or integrity anchor anywhere in the diff or repo (rg for 'example.com|install.sh' matches only this line).

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines send; races with close(results), loses results
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (f29743f) the body was `results <- j * 2` inside the loop, so Run blocked until every send completed — 'Run returned ⇒ all results delivered' was the working contract, and close(results) after return was safe. The diff wraps the send in `go func(j int)` (src/worker.go:7-9) and adds no WaitGroup, done channel, or count; Run falls off the loop and returns before any goroutine is known to have run. Any caller synchronizing on Run's return now races the in-flight sends: closing results after return panics ('send on closed channel'), a process that exits after Run returns silently drops results, and results no longer arrive in job order. This is a regression of an exported function's completion guarantee with no replacement synchronization offered.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutine sends complete; no WaitGroup
findings.whyItBreaks: Base 8b683ed made Run synchronous: on return, every result had been sent (verified via git show base:src/worker.go). Head spawns one unsynchronized goroutine per job (src/worker.go:7-9), so Run returns as soon as goroutines are merely spawned, with delivery state undefined. Every previously-correct caller pattern now breaks: (a) `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` races the pending sends → runtime panic 'send on closed channel'; (b) a caller that proceeds/exits after Run silently loses results while goroutines are mid-send; (c) a consumer that stops reading leaves up to len(jobs) goroutines blocked forever on send (leak the old synchronous backpressure made visible). No WaitGroup, done channel, or Wait API is added, so callers cannot even reconstruct the old guarantee. This is the package's entire exported surface; the contract change ships now, independent of in-repo callers (repo contains none).

findings.title: Ordered result delivery guarantee silently removed
findings.whyItBreaks: The unchanged exported carrier (`Run(ctx, jobs, results chan<- int)` @ src/worker.go:5) previously promised ordered, complete delivery: the k-th value read from `results` was jobs[k]*2 (base sent sequentially, verified via git show 8b683ed:src/worker.go). The new body implements none of that ordering — each goroutine (src/worker.go:7-9) contends for the channel in arbitrary schedule order. A caller that drains len(jobs) values and maps them positionally now receives values associated with the wrong jobs, silently — corrupted data with no error signal. Ordering is exactly the class of result-affecting promise whose removal on an exported path is a present defect even with no in-repo caller yet.

findings.title: Run returns before sends complete; close(results) after return now panics
findings.whyItBreaks: Run is an exported producer taking `results chan<- int`. Before this diff, Run returned only after every `results <- j*2` had completed, so the standard pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results); for v := range results` was safe and received all values in job order. Now Run returns immediately after spawning one goroutine per job, before any send is guaranteed. If the caller closes `results` after Run returns (the pattern the old semantics invited), in-flight goroutines send on a closed channel → unrecoverable `panic: send on closed channel` (process crash); if the close wins before goroutines schedule, results are silently lost. Results additionally arrive in nondeterministic order. As an exported API the prior completion guarantee was the contract; the body no longer implements it, so every caller's close/count/ordering logic is broken by construction (TRIGGER C: public carrier, promise affects the data a caller receives).

findings.title: Spawned goroutines ignore ctx and leak forever if consumer stops reading
findings.whyItBreaks: Each goroutine does an unconditional `results <- j * 2` with no `select` on `ctx.Done()`, and Run keeps no WaitGroup. If the consumer stops reading (e.g. its own ctx is cancelled), every spawned goroutine blocks on the channel send forever. Before this diff the blockage was confined to the caller's goroutine running Run; now Run returns success while N abandoned goroutines leak invisibly, so repeated calls (e.g. per-request in a server) accumulate unbounded blocked goroutines and memory with no cancellation or completion signal.

findings.title: Log accepts tag ...string but silently drops every tag from output
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER C, public carrier. The changed signature `func Log(message string, tag ...string)` promises that tags participate in the emitted log line — that is the only observable meaning of a tag parameter on a logging function. As an exported API, the promise itself is the contract; every eventual caller is forced to conflate 'tagged' with 'untagged'.

findings.title: buildReport mixes commits: builtFrom=branch ref but artifacts from "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, BuildReport satisfied the invariant artifacts === build.artifactsAt(builtFrom) by construction (both used `commit`, see base 7bc431d). The new code computes builtFrom from build.ref(branch) (src/report.ts:12) but resolves artifacts from build.ref("verified") (src/report.ts:13-14). For any Build implementation where the "verified" ref points to a different commit than the branch ref — the only scenario in which this edit changes output at all — the returned report pairs commit X as builtFrom with commit Y's artifacts. The unchanged carrier BuildReport { builtFrom; artifacts } promises the artifacts belong to the reported build; a consumer using builtFrom to reproduce, audit, or diff the artifact list silently gets a different commit's artifacts with no error. TRIGGER C: promises='artifacts of builtFrom' (interface fields, src/report.ts:8-9) vs body='artifactsAt(build.ref("verified"))' (src/report.ts:14) — mismatch; buildReport/formatArtifact have no in-repo callers (rg over repo), and buildReport is a public export, so the mismatched pairing is itself the defective data contract. Note: if "verified" always aliased the branch ref, the change would be a no-op — either way the line as written is wrong (inconsistent report) or pointless.

findings.title: buildReport pairs builtFrom with artifacts from hardcoded "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport is an exported function whose return contract pairs builtFrom (commit = build.ref(branch), line 12) with artifacts (line 14). The diff changed artifacts to build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")), so for any branch argument other than "verified" — the normal case, since branch is a free parameter of an exported API — the two fields describe different commits: builtFrom says commit C1 while the artifacts array contains C2's artifacts. The report is now internally contradictory on its primary path: a consumer using builtFrom as provenance for the artifacts list gets wrong-commit artifacts, and no field in BuildReport identifies which commit the artifacts actually came from. Even if "read artifacts at the verified ref" was the intent, builtFrom is then stale/misleading; either way the paired-field coherence the interface implies (builtFrom + artifacts as one build snapshot) is silently broken.

findings.title: Report mixes commits: builtFrom=ref(branch) but artifacts=artifactsAt(ref("verified"))
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport previously reported builtFrom and artifacts for the same commit (build.ref(branch)). The diff keeps builtFrom = build.ref(branch) but switches artifacts to build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). Additionally, the function now unconditionally dereferences a "verified" ref on every call, adding a hard precondition that did not exist before: any Build implementation without a "verified" ref (the interface only promises ref(name): string for arbitrary names) now fails or misbehaves where the old code succeeded for any existing branch. No in-repo caller, tests, or docs establish a 'verified'-ref protocol, so there is nothing telling callers this pairing changed.

findings.title: New `limit` parameter is ignored; build() always returns 10 items

findings.title: changedPaths computed at 'latest' but replayed on pinned fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The unchanged Changeset contract (src/changeset.ts:7-8) promises 'Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' At base, changedPaths = readChangedPaths(from) matched fromRevision = from. Now changedPaths = store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")) (line 18) while fromRevision stays store.resolve(pinnedTag) (line 17). For every call where resolve(pinnedTag) != resolve("latest") — the normal pinned-tag case — the returned changeset is self-inconsistent: consumers replay paths derived from 'latest' on top of the pinned revision. If readChangedPaths(rev) lists paths changed in/at rev, a path modified between the pinned tag and latest is replayed onto the pinned revision with the wrong base state (corrupt result); if it lists paths changed since rev, readChangedPaths(latest) yields a near-empty list and the changeset silently drops all changes. TRIGGER C: carrier = Changeset.fromRevision doc @src/changeset.ts:7-8; promises=changedPaths computed against fromRevision; body=readChangedPaths(resolve("latest")) @src/changeset.ts:18. buildChangeset is exported/public and the promised behavior (replay-base consistency) directly determines the data callers receive, so the absence of in-repo callers does not clear it.

The changed body breaks this: fromRevision = store.resolve(pinnedTag) (line 17) but changedPaths = store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")) (line 18). Substitution with a pinned tag whose resolution differs from 'latest' (the exact scenario the pinnedTag parameter exists for): fromRevision=rev(A), changedPaths=paths of rev(B≠A) → the consumer replays rev-B's changed path set on top of rev-A, applying the wrong changes. This is silent data corruption on the function's core path, not a no-op: if pinnedTag always resolved to 'latest', both the parameter and the change would be pointless.

findings.title: changedPaths computed at 'latest' but fromRevision records pinned revision

findings.title: Cache key ignores tenantId — tenants get each other's settings
findings.whyItBreaks: `settingsFor(tenantId, name, store)` is per-tenant by contract: tenantId is a required parameter and is forwarded to `store.fetch(tenantId, name)` (src/settings.ts:15), so values are tenant-specific. The new `cacheKey(name)` returns `settings:${name}` (line 8) with no tenant component, so the guard at lines 13-14 (`hit !== undefined`) serves the first tenant's fetched value to every subsequent tenant. Substitution: settingsFor('t1','quota') → miss → fetch('t1','quota')='100' → cache['settings:quota']='100'; then settingsFor('t2','quota') → cache hit at line 13-14 → returns '100' to tenant t2 without ever calling fetch for t2. Cross-tenant wrong-value + data exposure; whichever tenant fetches first after `invalidate(name)` (line 20-22) wins for all tenants, and per-tenant invalidation is now impossible because the API dropped tenantId. The asymmetry (tenantId kept in fetch, removed only from the key) shows this is a regression, not a single-tenant redesign. Fix: restore the tenant-scoped key and signature.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId — cross-tenant setting values collide and leak
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}`, omitting tenantId, and settingsFor now uses it for both the hit check (line 12-13) and the set (line 16) while still fetching per-tenant via store.fetch(tenantId, name) (line 15). Substitution: tenant A reads name="rate_limit" → miss → cache.set("settings:rate_limit", "100"); tenant B then reads name="rate_limit" → cache hit at line 13 returns "100" — tenant A's value — without store.fetch("tenantB", ...) ever being called. Every tenant sharing a setting name with another tenant silently receives the first-cached tenant's configuration: unauthorized cross-tenant data disclosure plus wrong-value integrity corruption on the core settings path. Before this diff the key was `${tenantId}:${name}`, which isolated tenants correctly.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}`, dropping tenantId, and both the write (cache.set @ line 16) and the read (cache.get @ line 13) use it. findings.title: Async reserve() breaks atomicity: concurrent calls oversell the last unit
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, reserve() was synchronous: read stock (line 15), guard (line 16), decrement (line 18) had no yield point, so in JS's single-threaded model the check-then-act was atomic. This diff adds `await this.store.save(...)` at line 17 between the guard and the decrement. Trace with stock={'sku1': 1}: call A reads remaining=1, passes the guard, suspends in save(); call B then reads remaining=1 (memory not yet decremented), also passes the guard and suspends; A resumes, sets stock=0, returns true; B resumes, sets stock=0, returns true. Both callers hold a reservation for one unit — the boolean contract ('true = you reserved it') is violated for one of them, and the persisted value saved twice (0) records only a single decrement, so the store cannot reconcile the two grants either. The exported public method is now inherently concurrently invokable (async reservation APIs are used from concurrent HTTP handlers), so this is a live oversell path, not theory.

findings.title: Await inside reserve() breaks atomic check-then-decrement, allowing oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() previously performed read-check-write synchronously, which JS run-to-run semantics made atomic: with stock=1 only one caller could observe remaining=1. The diff inserts `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) between the guard (line 16) and `this.stock.set` (line 18). Every await yields, so a second concurrent reserve() for the same SKU executes during the first one's save window, reads the stale remaining=1, also passes the guard, and both calls return true while persisting 0 — one unit is reserved twice. Concurrency is the normal operating mode for an inventory reservation API, so this silently reintroduces the exact oversell the boolean contract exists to prevent.

findings.title: Async reserve introduces check-then-act race; concurrent calls over-reserve
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous reserve() was fully synchronous and therefore atomic under JS's single-threaded execution. This diff inserts `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) between the stock guard (lines 15-16) and the decrement (line 18). During the suspension a second reserve('x') call runs, reads the same stale `remaining`, passes the same `remaining <= 0` guard, and persists the same `remaining - 1`. With stock=1 both calls return true (two reservations granted for one unit; store saved sku->0 twice) — a double-sell. With larger stock both calls write the identical stale `remaining - 1`, so the second decrement is lost (e.g. stock 2 + two concurrent calls ends at stock 1 instead of 0). The save-failure path is fine (rejection propagates, memory untouched), but the concurrency path is broken.

findings.title: retry.ts still multiplies backoff() by 1000 after unit change to ms

findings.title: Save() now discards f.Close() error; close-time write failures return nil
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code propagated the close error to callers via `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24). The head replaces it with `defer f.Close()` on line 13; because the function returns `w.Flush()` directly, the Close error is dropped with no way to reach the caller. Close on a file opened for writing can fail after Flush succeeded (ENOSPC/EIO surfaced at close, e.g. NFS or delayed-allocation filesystems). Save is an exported API of package store (no in-repo callers yet, which makes it worse, not better): every caller is forced to conflate a failed persist with a successful one — it will report success and treat the file as durable when it may be truncated/unflushed. This is a removed error-propagation branch (TRIGGER D swallow site).

findings.title: Save() discards f.Close() error on success path via defer f.Close()
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version ended the success path with `return f.Close()` — the only place the Close error was propagated. Now `defer f.Close()` discards it and Save returns w.Flush(), which is nil on success. Since w.Flush() only pushes bytes to the OS, close(2) is the last point at which deferred writeback failures (EIO, ENOSPC, NFS/quota errors) are reported. On such a failure Save now returns nil while the file's data was never durably written — silent data loss for every caller of this exported package API.

findings.title: Save discards f.Close() error; close-failure is reported as success
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code propagated the close error to the caller on every path (explicit f.Close() + `return f.Close()` on success). The diff swaps this for `defer f.Close()`, whose error is discarded, and returns only `w.Flush()` (store/save.go:19). Close on a written file can fail after Flush 'succeeds' (delayed I/O errors, NFS, quota enforcement at close); in that case Save now returns nil and every caller of this exported API treats lost/unpersisted data as durably saved. Failure and success are no longer distinguishable at the caller boundary — the swallow is baked into the contract, not a future-caller concern.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_window drops the last row of every page

Substitution: rows=[a,b,c], page_index=0, page_size=3 gives start=0, end=3; old code returned [a,b,c], new code returns [a,b]. Worse, for 10 rows at page_size=3 the last page (page_index=3) computes start=9, end=10 and renders an empty page, so summarize drops row 10 from all output entirely while page_count still counts that page — silent data loss in rendered output on every page.

Degenerate case rows=['a'], page_size=1: start=0, end=1, range(0,0) yields [] — the entire page disappears. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) both consume this window, so every rendered page silently omits its final row while the row numbering for surviving rows looks normal — a silent, user-visible truncation with no error signal.

findings.title: Inverted TTL comparison: cache serves stale values forever and never serves fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from '<' (base, fresh→hit) to '>'. Substitution with real values: set() stores storedAt=Date.now() (src/cache.ts:12); an immediate get() computes age≈0, and 0 > ttlMs is false, so the fresh entry falls through to entries.delete() (src/cache.ts:21) and returns null — a value can NEVER be served while it is fresh. Conversely, once age > ttlMs the branch returns entry.value (src/cache.ts:19) and skips the delete, so expired entries are served indefinitely and never evicted. Every consumer receives stale data forever and cache misses for fresh data; the cache's core contract (fresh→hit, expired→miss) is fully inverted.

findings.title: splice() inside forEach() skips the element shifted into the visited index
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach advances the index after each callback, but splice(index, 1) shifts the following element into that index, so it is never visited. Substitution: input [{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}] → k=0 is done, splice → array becomes [{done:true},{done:false}]; k=1 visits the element shifted from index 2 ({done:false}), not done; k=2 is now past the shortened length. Result: [{done:true},{done:false}] — the second done job survives pruning. Any run of two or more adjacent done jobs leaves done jobs in the queue.

findings.title: pruneDone changed from pure filter to in-place mutation of the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function's contract (name, signature, and base implementation `return jobs.filter(...)` at 3746a0b:src/queue.ts:7) promises a non-mutating prune that returns a filtered copy. The body now splices the input array in place and returns the same reference, so every caller's retained list is silently stripped of done jobs and `result !== jobs` no longer holds. This is a public exported module with no in-repo callers: the broken promise is the shipped API contract itself — any caller upgrading sees its source list mutated as a side effect of a call that previously had none.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check: get() serves expired entries, evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed predicate at src/cache.ts:18 flips the freshness test. After this diff, get() returns entry.value when Date.now()-storedAt > ttlMs — i.e. it returns the value only once it is EXPIRED, and because that branch never deletes the entry, the stale value is served forever. A FRESH entry (elapsed <= ttlMs) takes the fall-through branch, is deleted at src/cache.ts:21, and get() returns null. So every read of valid cached data now misses and destroys the entry, and every expired value is served indefinitely. Base (e9ed801) used '<', which was correct.

findings.title: splice inside forEach skips the job after each removal; done jobs survive
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach fixes its iteration range and index progression up front (ECMA-262), but splice shifts subsequent elements left. The element immediately after a removed one is never examined. Repro: pruneDone([{id:'a',done:true},{id:'b',done:true},{id:'c',done:false}]) — k=0 removes 'a', array becomes [b,c]; k=1 examines 'c' (not done); k=2 is out of range. Result keeps done job 'b'. The function's sole purpose (remove ALL done jobs) fails for any two adjacent done jobs; the base implementation (filter) handled this correctly.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness predicate was flipped from `<` to `>`. Substitution: entry stored at T, ttlMs=60000, read at T+1s (fresh, age 1000): `1000 > 60000` is false → entry is DELETED and get returns null, so a fresh read destroys the cached value. Read at T+61s (expired): `61000 > 60000` is true → stale value is returned and the entry is kept forever. The cache now behaves anti-correctly: fresh data is lost and stale data is served. Base (f81d7bc) line 18 `<` had the correct semantics.

findings.title: splice inside forEach skips consecutive done jobs, leaving them unpruned
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element while Array.prototype.forEach iterates shifts later elements left and the index counter still advances, so the element that moves into the just-visited index is never checked. Substitution with [A(done),B(done),C(done)]: visit idx0 → splice A → array [B,C]; next visit is idx1 → C (B was shifted into idx0 and is never visited) → splice C → result [B(done)]. The function whose sole purpose is removing done jobs returns done jobs whenever two or more are adjacent — the common case after a batch finishes. Base (f81d7bc) used `filter`, which is correct.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array and returns the same reference
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported public function changed from pure (filter returned a new array, input untouched) to aliasing: it splices the caller's array in place and returns that same reference, so `pruneDone(j) === j` changed from false to true. Any caller that retains the original list (status display, retry pass, logging) silently loses the done jobs from it — caller data is mutated as a side effect with no signature or doc change signaling it.

findings.title: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff deletes `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` (present at base 40c4c1f, verified via git show). On empty input, `rows.reduce((sum,row)=>sum+row.amount, 0)` yields 0 and `0 / rows.length` evaluates to 0/0 = NaN. averageAmount is an exported public function taking a plain Row[], so an empty dataset is a legitimate input; every caller previously got the defined value 0 and now gets NaN, which silently poisons downstream arithmetic (sums→NaN, comparisons→false, JSON.stringify(NaN)→null) instead of surfacing any signal.

findings.title: busiest() sorts caller's array in place (input mutation)
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff replaces `[...rows].sort(...)` (base 40c4c1f, verified via git show) with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort mutates the receiver, so this exported query function now silently reorders the caller's array as a side effect of asking for the busiest row. Any caller that keeps using its rows afterwards (rendering, persistence, iteration) observes a destroyed order; under equal amounts the reordering is arbitrary. The defensive copy existed precisely to prevent this; deleting it is a regression of the function's contract as a pure lookup.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. Substituting rows=[]: reduce with init 0 yields total=0, then line 8 computes 0/0 = NaN. The exported signature promises `number`; callers previously got a well-defined 0 for empty input and now silently get NaN, which propagates through any arithmetic and serializes to null via JSON, corrupting downstream stats/persistence without any error signal.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array in place (drop the spread copy)

Any caller that reads `rows` afterwards (render order, index-based access, further aggregation by position) sees corrupted order; the function's return value does not reveal the side effect.

findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. For an empty array, reduce((sum,row)=>sum+row.amount, 0) yields 0, then `0 / rows.length` computes 0/0 = NaN. This is an exported public function whose defined behavior for empty input was 0; every caller passing an empty result set (e.g., a period with no rows) now receives NaN, which poisons downstream arithmetic, fails all comparisons (NaN !== NaN), and renders as 'NaN' in reports. Substitution performed: rows=[] → total=0 @line7 → 0/0 → NaN @line8 (previously 0).

findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)[0] ?? null`. Array.prototype.sort sorts in place and returns the same array reference, so this exported query function now reorders the caller's array as a side effect. Any caller that passes a list it still reads in original order (e.g., render a table, then compute busiest) silently gets its data shuffled. The dropped defensive copy changes a pure lookup into a mutating operation with no signature or doc change to warn callers.

findings.title: sort() without comparator orders scores as strings; leaderboard returns wrong players
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts by UTF-16 code units (ECMA-262 SortCompare default). The diff replaces `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)` (base 13bf047, line 8) with `scores.sort(); scores.reverse();`. Substitution: players with scores [9, 10], n=1 → sort() yields [10, 9] because "10" < "9" lexicographically → reverse → [9, 10] → cutoff = scores[0] = 9 → filter keeps both players → slice(0,1) returns the score-9 player. Base returned the score-10 player. Likewise [2, 100, 20], n=1 → sort()→[100,20,2]→reverse→[2,20,100] → cutoff=2 → returns the score-2 player instead of score-100. Every score set where lexicographic and numeric order diverge (any mix of digit counts, i.e. any score ≥ 10 alongside a smaller one) yields a wrong cutoff in topPlayers (src/leaderboard.ts:15-16) and a wrong rendered board via the exported formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20).

findings.title: sort() without comparator is lexicographic; reverse() does not restore numeric order
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts by code units, so [2,10,9] sorts to [10,2,9]; reversing yields [9,2,10], not the numeric descending [10,9,2] the base code produced with `sort((a,b)=>b-a)`. Substitution in the consumer: players a=2,b=10,c=9, n=2 → rankScores @src/leaderboard.ts:6-11 returns [9,2,10] → cutoff @src/leaderboard.ts:15 = scores[1] = 2 → filter keeps all three, slice(0,2) returns [a(2), b(10)], ranking a score-2 player first and dropping the score-9 player. Worse, for [5,10] n=1: sort() gives [10,5], reverse gives [5,10], cutoff=scores[0]=5 → returns the score-5 player instead of score-10. Exported public API `topPlayers` and its consumer `formatBoard` @src/leaderboard.ts:20 emit wrong leaderboards for any score mix spanning digit counts (e.g. 9 vs 10) or negatives ("-10" < "-5" lexically too).

findings.title: sort() without numeric comparator breaks descending order; wrong top-N cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)` with `scores.sort()` + `scores.reverse()`. JS `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator converts elements to strings and orders by UTF-16 code units, so the array is not in descending numeric order. Substitution with real values: scores=[1,5,10,100] → sort() → [1,10,100,5] → reverse → [5,100,10,1]. In topPlayers (src/leaderboard.ts:15), cutoff = scores[Math.min(2,4)-1] = 100 instead of the correct 2nd-largest 10; filter+slice returns only [100] instead of [100,10] — a legitimate top-2 entry is dropped. Worse: scores=[2,10], n=1 → sort() → [10,2] → reverse → [2,10] → cutoff=scores[0]=2 → both players pass the filter and slice(0,1) returns the score-2 player as #1 (wrong winner). Any leaderboard with scores of mixed digit counts (the normal case) produces wrong results via export topPlayers (line 13) and its caller formatBoard (line 20).

findings.title: Signature verify uses '==' instead of compare_digest (timing attack)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code compared the computed HMAC hex digest to given_signature with hmac.compare_digest, which is constant-time. The diff replaces it with plain '=='; CPython's str equality short-circuits at the first differing character, so verify()'s wall-clock time correlates with the length of the correct prefix of the attacker-supplied signature (CWE-208). verify() is the only gate on handle() (app/webhook.py:14): a forged signature yields status 200 and executes processor(payload) on attacker-controlled data; a wrong one yields 401. An attacker with network access to the endpoint can recover the SHA-256 hex digest byte-by-byte via statistical timing of many 401 responses, then forge arbitrary webhook payloads that pass authentication. The hmac module is still imported (app/webhook.py:2), so restoring constant-time comparison is trivial.

findings.title: Signature verify uses non-constant-time '==', enabling timing attacks
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the sole authentication gate for webhook payloads: handle() (app/webhook.py:14) executes processor(payload) and returns 200 only when verify() passes. The diff replaced hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature. Plain '==' on the hex digest strings is not constant time — comparison cost varies with the number of leading matching characters — so a remote attacker can iteratively forge given_signature byte-by-byte via measured response timing and eventually reach the 200 branch, executing the processor with an unauthenticated payload. This is exactly the vulnerability class hmac.compare_digest exists to prevent, and the base version had it; this PR is a direct regression of that defense on a live auth path.

findings.title: verify() uses non-constant-time == on MAC, enabling timing forgery
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version compared the computed HMAC with hmac.compare_digest (constant-time). The new code compares signature_of(payload, secret) (a hex digest str, built at app/webhook.py:6) to given_signature with ==, which short-circuits on the first differing character and leaks timing. verify() is the sole auth gate: handle() at app/webhook.py:14 rejects with 401 only when verify() is False, and on success executes processor(payload) (app/webhook.py:16). An attacker can exploit the timing oracle to recover the expected signature byte-by-byte across repeated requests, then forge validly signed webhook payloads that get processed — a direct regression of an existing security control. (Accept/reject sets are unchanged, so this is purely the side channel, not a logic change.)

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction break transfer atomicity (data loss)
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (d8fdece), the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled back all three. The refactor commits the ledger INSERT when the `with` block exits (app/transfer.py:22-23), then runs `_apply_balances` afterwards with no transaction. The two UPDATEs now execute in separate implicit transactions. Concrete failure paths introduced by this diff: (1) the debit UPDATE succeeds and the credit UPDATE fails or the process crashes between statements → source account is debited, destination never credited, money destroyed; (2) `_apply_balances` raises (connection drop, DB error) → the exception propagates and the caller sees a failed transfer, but the ledger row is already durably committed recording a transfer that never happened; retrying the call double-records the ledger entry. Every rollback guarantee this function previously had for the balance mutation is removed.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction: partial transfer persists on failure
findings.whyItBreaks: In base, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block — all-or-nothing. In head, only `_record_ledger` runs inside the block (line 23); `_apply_balances` executes at line 24 after the transaction has committed. Two concrete corruption paths: (1) if `_apply_balances` raises after the ledger insert committed (connection loss, constraint trigger, process kill), the ledger row permanently records a transfer whose balances were never applied — the exception propagates to the caller but the committed ledger entry cannot be rolled back; (2) the debit UPDATE (line 11-14) and credit UPDATE (line 15-18) now run as separate uncovered statements, so a failure or crash between them persists debit-without-credit, destroying funds. This is a money-transfer atomicity regression introduced by this diff.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Base executed the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs inside `with db.transaction():`, so any failure rolled back all three. Head commits the ledger INSERT (line 23) and only then calls `_apply_balances` (line 24) outside the transaction: (1) if either UPDATE raises (constraint violation, lock timeout, crash between statements), the ledger row stays committed while balances are unchanged — ledger and balances permanently diverge; (2) the debit (lines 10-12) and credit (lines 14-16) UPDATEs themselves run outside any transaction, so the first can persist without the second, destroying funds; (3) the caller contract silently changed — an exception from `transfer()` no longer guarantees nothing was persisted.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to host-local date components
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body computed the billing day from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate (verified via git show 963e727:src/billing/day.ts); the new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the host process's local timezone. Substitution on TZ=America/New_York: for at = 2025-06-15T02:30:00Z, old output = "2025-06-15", new output = "2025-06-14". Consequences: (1) billing-day keys become deployment-environment-dependent — the same instant buckets to different days on UTC vs non-UTC hosts; (2) sameBillingDay (line 8) classification flips: the pair (2025-06-15T02:30:00Z, 2025-06-15T23:00:00Z) was same-day (true) under UTC and is now different-day (false), moving usage-group boundaries; (3) any billing-day string persisted or compared under the old UTC semantics becomes inconsistent after upgrade. The exported function is a public contract; the commit carries no message, test, or TZ configuration indicating an intentional local-time policy, so the change silently alters billing period assignment.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local-time accessors, not UTC, shifting day buckets
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation deliberately used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; this diff replaces all three with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the returned key now depends on the process timezone (TZ env / host locale) instead of being deterministic per instant. Substitution: with TZ=America/New_York, billingDay(new Date('2026-03-01T02:30:00Z')) returns '2026-02-28' (local Feb 28 21:30) where the old code returned '2026-03-01'; with TZ=Asia/Tokyo, billingDay(new Date('2026-03-01T20:00:00Z')) returns '2026-03-02' vs '2026-03-01'. Any key persisted under the old UTC scheme no longer matches on upgrade, and sameBillingDay (line 8) now classifies two instants on the same UTC day as different billing days whenever a local midnight falls between them (e.g. 02:30Z and 04:00Z on 2026-03-01 in New York: '2026-02-28' vs '2026-03-01'), breaking day-based dedup/attribution. Host-local wall time is not a defensible billing contract — it changes per deployment/region; if a non-UTC business timezone were intended it would need to be an explicit parameter.

findings.title: billingDay silently switched from UTC to local-time getters
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite replaces getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. Day bucketing is now dependent on the host timezone: e.g. timestamp 2026-09-10T02:00:00Z returned '2026-09-10' at base (UTC), but on a host in America/New_York (UTC-4) the new code returns '2026-09-09'. Any consumer aggregating or deduplicating per billing day (including sameBillingDay at src/billing/day.ts:8, which compares billingDay(a)===billingDay(b)) silently re-buckets events near UTC midnight, and results are nondeterministic across environments (dev vs prod TZ). This is a silent semantic regression disguised as a refactor.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenant: cross-tenant account collision returns wrong profile
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level Map shared by all callers. With key = account (line 14), a cache hit short-circuits the tenant-scoped fetch: readProfile('t1','shared') caches under 'shared'; a later readProfile('t2','shared') hits at line 15-16 and returns the t1 Profile without ever calling fetchProfile('t2','shared'). The returned Profile.tenant ('t1') contradicts the requested tenant ('t2') — the signature at lines 9-13 promises a profile scoped to (tenant, account), and the tenant argument is now ignored on any hit. Account names are caller-supplied free strings, so collisions across tenants are ordinary, and the leak is silent (no error, wrong displayName/tenant data returned). Before this change the key `${tenant}:${account}` enforced isolation.

findings.title: Cache key dropped tenant: cross-tenant profile collision in readProfile
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile's identity is (tenant, account) — it fetches via fetchProfile(tenant, account) and returns a Profile carrying that tenant. The memo key was `${tenant}:${account}` and is now just `account`, so any two calls with different tenants and the same account map to one cache entry. Substitution: readProfile('t1','alice') caches profile {tenant:'t1'} under key 'alice'; a later readProfile('t2','alice') hits memo.get('alice') @src/profile.ts:15 and returns t1's profile (wrong tenant/displayName) without ever calling fetchProfile for t2 — deterministic wrong data returned, and the wrong entry persists for the process lifetime since `memo` is module-level.

findings.title: Drop tenant from memo key causes cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile's memo (module-level Map, src/profile.ts:7) is process-wide, and both the function signature and fetchProfile(tenant, account) (src/profile.ts:12,17) treat profiles as tenant-scoped. After this change the key is `account` alone. Substitution: readProfile("tenantA","acct1",f) fetches and stores memo["acct1"]=profileA (line 18); a later readProfile("tenantB","acct1",f) hits memo.get("acct1") at line 15 and returns tenantA's Profile (tenantA's displayName/data) for tenantB — silently, without ever calling fetchProfile for tenantB. Tenant is still accepted as a parameter but no longer affects the cached result for any tenant after the first. That is a tenant-isolation bypass (confidentiality leak) plus guaranteed wrong data whenever two tenants share an account identifier (e.g. "default", "primary"). Exported public symbol, so every eventual caller is exposed.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty-string fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff wraps load() in try/catch and returns "" on failure. A Map<string,string> can legitimately hold "" as a value, so load('present', new Map([['present','']])) and load('missing', store) are now indistinguishable — both return "". The error signal that previously propagated to the caller (base src/store.ts:3) is discarded, not logged, and not part of any documented contract. The in-repo consumer loadAll (src/store.ts:12) previously threw on the first missing key; it now silently pads its result array with "" entries for missing keys, so a caller processing loadAll output acts on failure-as-value exactly as it would on real empty data.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error into empty-string return
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). Base behavior: load() threw Error(`missing: <key>`) (src/store.ts:4), which propagated to every caller, so failure was loud and named the missing key. Head behavior: the new catch at src/store.ts:6-8 intercepts that same throw and returns "". Precondition substitution: changed value "" → consumer loadAll (src/store.ts:12, keys.map((k) => load(k, store)), unchanged) → no guard reads it, it is placed directly in the returned array → a missing key now yields "" in the output slot, indistinguishable from a key present with value "". load() is an exported public function; its contract previously guaranteed missing keys are never returned as values. Every caller is now forced to treat failure as a real value — on this file's own live path, loadAll can no longer fail fast or report which key was missing, and neither can any external consumer of the module. The error signal (including the key name in the message) is discarded without even a log, so failure is not distinguishable at any decision point.

findings.title: load() catch-all converts missing-key error into "" — failure indistinguishable from real value
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (cd0b100), `load` propagated `Error("missing: <key>")` to callers for any absent key. The head wraps the body in try/catch and returns "" (src/store.ts:6-7), so the failure signal is downgraded to a default value that is identical to a legitimately stored empty string. The internal throw at src/store.ts:4 is now dead machinery — thrown only to be instantly swallowed. Every caller is forced to conflate 'key missing' with value "": the in-repo consumer `loadAll` (src/store.ts:12) now silently returns `['', '']` for entirely-absent keys instead of throwing, so any downstream persistence, rendering, or computation built on the result treats the failure as real data. As an exported API, every eventual external caller inherits this unusable contract — failure and legitimate "" are indistinguishable at every decision point.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all errors; void return conflates success with total failure
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D, added public path. The new exported function wraps every fn() invocation in `catch { continue; }` (src/retry.ts:25-26) and returns void on both success (early `return` at :24) and exhaustion (deadline bail at :23 or loop end at :27). All N failure signals are discarded: previously_reached=n/a (this is a newly added public path — no propagation ever existed; the error signal is created by fn() and destroyed inside the function), now_receives=`undefined`/void at every call site. No caller can write a branch that distinguishes 'fn succeeded' from 'all attempts threw' or 'deadline hit before any attempt', so callers are forced to treat total failure as success — persisting, reporting, or proceeding on work that never happened. This is not cleared by the identical pre-existing pattern in retry() (unchanged code, out of scope here) and nothing documents void-on-failure as the contract; no logging preserves the signal. Per the swallow-site carve-out this is a present contract defect even with zero in-repo callers (verified: rg finds no importers). Minimal fix: return a boolean (or throw the last caught error) so failure remains distinguishable.

findings.title: Split Config contract: retry ignores retries; retryBackground ignores maxAttempts
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER C on the changed public carrier. The diff makes Config require BOTH `maxAttempts` (:2) and `retries` (:3), but the two same-signature exported functions each read exactly one bound: retry loops on `config.maxAttempts` (src/retry.ts:9) and silently ignores `retries`; retryBackground loops on `config.retries` (src/retry.ts:22) and silently ignores `maxAttempts`. Substitution on a legitimate caller: `retry(fn, { maxAttempts: 3, retries: 0, timeout: 5000 })` — caller expresses 'no retries' via retries: 0, yet fn executes up to 3 times because the field governing retry() is the other one; symmetrically `retryBackground(fn, { maxAttempts: 1, retries: 10, timeout: 5000 })` runs 10 attempts. Every call site must therefore carry one required field that is silently dead, with no type-level or runtime signal of which field governs which function — the type promises both bounds govern, the bodies implement only one each (promise ≠ implementation; affects the number of fn() executions the caller receives). Root cause is that retryBackground (lines 20-27) is a byte-for-byte duplicate of retry() except for the loop-bound field — duplicated behavior instead of parameterizing the existing retry(). Verified no in-repo callers/tests exist (single-file repo), so no compile error surfaces the dead field.

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry but reads a different required Config field
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground (src/retry.ts:20-31) is byte-identical to retry (src/retry.ts:7-18) except line 22 loops on config.retries where line 9 loops on config.maxAttempts. Both fields are required on the shared exported Config (src/retry.ts:2-3), and each function silently ignores one of them. Substitution with Config{maxAttempts:5, retries:1, timeout:1000}: retry invokes fn up to 5 times, retryBackground invokes it once and gives up. A caller passing one config to both (the type actively encourages this) gets silently different retry behavior, and a caller of retryBackground who names the field as documented — 'retries' meaning attempts after the first, per the module's own maxAttempts naming — loses an attempt (line 22 counts the first fn() call against retries, i.e. retries:3 yields 3 total attempts, not 1+3). No compile error flags any of this.

findings.title: retryBackground verbatim-duplicates retry; split Config loop bounds
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground (lines 20-31) is byte-identical to retry (lines 7-18) except it bounds its loop on config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts, while both read the same shared Config in which BOTH fields are required (lines 2-3). retry(fn, { maxAttempts: n, timeout: t }) already provides exactly this capability. Any caller of retryBackground must also supply a maxAttempts value that is silently ignored, and vice versa: retryBackground(fn, { maxAttempts: 5, retries: 1, timeout: 1000 }) runs once while the specified maxAttempts: 5 is dead. Two exported copies with divergent required config keys guarantee wrong retry counts and independent drift.

findings.title: value.length on string|number union: compile error + 'len=undefined' render
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 2 widens the exported FieldProps.value to `string | number`, but line 6 evaluates `value.length`. Two concrete failures: (1) `length` does not exist on `number`, so the file no longer typechecks — tsc rejects line 6 with TS2339 (Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'), breaking any typechecked build of this public component; (2) at runtime, callers passing the now type-admitted `number` get `value.length === undefined`, so line 7 renders `<input defaultValue="len=undefined">` — garbage output for every valid number input. The defect holds regardless of whether the new 'len=N' display is the intended feature: the number branch is broken under either intent. TRIGGER C: carrier = exported FieldProps.value annotation @src/components/Field.tsx:2; promises = component accepts and correctly renders string | number; body = `value.length` @src/components/Field.tsx:6 implements no number handling; callers = none in repo (git grep: Field.tsx is the only source file) but the API is exported and the promised behavior affects the rendered result callers receive.

Additionally, for existing string callers the rendered content silently changed from the value itself to its length, breaking every current consumer of this exported component.

Substitution with a real value from the newly admitted type: value=42 → (42).length === undefined → label = "len=undefined" → the input renders "len=undefined" instead of anything derived from the value. findings.title: Stop echoing the TOKEN secret value into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step binds secrets.TOKEN to env TOKEN and runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, deliberately writing the secret value into the job log. The only thing preventing disclosure is GitHub's runtime masking of exact secret strings; masking is a backstop, not a contract — it silently fails the moment the value is transformed (encoded, truncated, interpolated into a URL) and it is the sole barrier if the log is readable by third parties (repo visibility cannot be verified from the checkout). The workflow runs on every push, so the secret is exposed to the step's full script environment on all builds. A senior reviewer should block printing a secret in a deploy workflow even when current output is masked.

findings.title: Remove echo of secrets.TOKEN into workflow log
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step maps secrets.TOKEN into env and its sole action is `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, interpolating the secret value into the Actions run log. GitHub's automatic log masking is best-effort exact-match redaction: it is documented to fail for numeric-only or short secrets and for any transformed rendering, and logs are retained and readable by everyone with read access to the repo's Actions history. If TOKEN does not mask (format unknown), the deploy credential is exposed verbatim in persisted logs. Printing secrets to logs is itself the defect per GitHub's security hardening guidance; the step provides no deployment functionality, so there is no offsetting benefit.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into the deploy job log
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step maps secrets.TOKEN to env TOKEN and runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, deliberately writing the secret value to the workflow log. GitHub only redacts it via best-effort runtime masking (exact-match substitution with ***), which the GitHub security-hardening docs explicitly warn is not guaranteed (multi-line tokens, tokens with characters the runner shell/log processor transforms, or any future tweak like ${TOKEN:0:8} or base64-encoding leak silently). Logs are retained ~90 days and readable by everyone with read access to the repo, so the echo creates a standing, unnecessary disclosure surface with zero functional benefit — the secret is not consumed by `make build`. The `on: push` trigger means it fires on every push. A strict reviewer blocks this before merge even though masking usually holds.

findings.title: Dropping maxBuffer from git() makes diffs >1 MiB fail the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (the removed option was 64 MiB). When a child's stdout exceeds maxBuffer, Node kills it (SIGTERM/ENOBUFS), sets res.status=null, and truncates output — so the pre-existing status!==0 check at line 38 throws 'git diff ... failed:' with empty stderr. The full PR patch is produced by this same helper at line 140 (git diff mergeBase headSha), and changedFileSet uses it at line 57. Any PR whose diff text exceeds 1 MiB (lockfile churn, generated code, mass renames) previously reviewed fine and now always aborts: the catch at the end of runGithub posts the 'Needlefish: review errored and did NOT pass this PR' check and sets exitCode=1, blocking the workflow. The sibling helpers gh()/ghText() still pass maxBuffer 64 MiB, confirming this drop is accidental, not a deliberate normalization.

findings.title: git() loses 64MiB maxBuffer; PR diffs over 1MiB now hard-fail
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's 1MiB default (1048576 bytes). git() runs the full PR patch at src/adapters/github.ts:140 (`git diff mergeBase headSha`) and the file list at :57; any PR whose diff exceeds 1MiB (lockfiles, generated files — the gh() helpers at :19/:29 keep 64MiB precisely for this) makes spawnSync kill the child with ENOBUFS, so res.status is null (null !== 0) and the function throws with an empty stderr message. The whole review then aborts via the catch at :182, posting 'Needlefish: review failed' on PRs that reviewed fine before this change — a regression introduced by this diff.

findings.title: bundle.baseSha no longer the merge-base the patch was computed against
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is set (the normal Actions wiring these lines exist for), baseSha is the base-branch tip, not the common ancestor. patch (:140, `git diff mergeBase headSha`) and changedFiles (:141, changedFileSet on mergeBase) are both computed from mergeBase (:139), but the bundle now ships baseSha instead of mergeBase. Substitution: base advanced since the PR branched (common on active repos) → `git diff baseSha headSha != patch` and `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD != changedFiles`; a consumer that derives the reviewed diff from bundle.baseSha..headSha (the purpose of carrying base+head SHAs) reviews other people's merged commits, and any checkout/apply of patch against baseSha can fail to apply because patch context comes from the merge-base tree. The previously shipped mergeBase guaranteed baseSha/patch/changedFiles consistency; this change breaks that invariant in the bundle's public contract. When PR_BASE_SHA is unset the fallback yields baseSha == mergeBase, so the change is a no-op only on that path.

findings.title: Dropping maxBuffer from git() breaks reviews for patches >1 MiB
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (1048576, verified). git() is used at line 140 to fetch the full PR patch (`git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>`) and at line 57 for the changed-file list. For any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB, Node kills the child (ENOBUFS, res.status = null), the `res.status !== 0` check throws, and runGithub's catch posts a 'Needlefish: review failed' check and exits 1. The previous 64 MiB budget (still deliberately present on gh()/ghText() at lines 9 and 21) made such PRs reviewable. This is a regression introduced by this diff on the primary code path of the adapter.

findings.title: Bundle pairs patch (merge-base diff) with baseSha (base-branch tip)
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 138 sets baseSha from PR_BASE_SHA (the base branch tip in Actions); line 139 computes mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha); lines 140–141 build patch and changedFiles from mergeBase. The old code exported `baseSha: mergeBase`, guaranteeing bundle.baseSha was the commit the patch was diffed against. Now, whenever the base branch has advanced past the PR's fork point (baseSha not an ancestor of headSha), the bundle declares baseSha = B while patch = diff(M, H) with M = merge-base(B, H). Any consumer recomputing diff(B, H), reading pre-images via `git show B:path`, or assuming the patch applies onto B gets divergent content: diff(B, H) additionally contains the inverse of the B..M commits that landed on the base branch, and the patch's pre-image/context comes from M. The delivered artifact is internally inconsistent by construction. (When PR_BASE_SHA is unset, merge-base(M, H) === M, so behavior is unchanged there.)

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox pin dropped from codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd=opts.repoPath and a prompt fed on stdin. Before this change the args array pinned `-s read-only`, forcing the sandbox policy regardless of environment. After the change, no sandbox flag is passed, so the codex CLI resolves the sandbox from `~/.codex/config.toml` (`sandbox_mode` setting / layered profiles) — confirmed by the installed codex-cli 0.153.4 help, which lists `read-only | workspace-write | danger-full-access` for `-s` and offers `--ignore-user-config` specifically to skip config.toml, proving config is otherwise loaded. On any machine whose config sets `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `"danger-full-access"`, model-generated commands driven by an untrusted, PR/repo-derived prompt can now mutate the repository under review (workspace-write) or gain unrestricted disk and network access (danger-full-access, enabling exfiltration). The prior flag was the only privilege guard on this path — the function exposes no env var or option to control the sandbox (unlike bin via CODEX_BIN and model via CODEX_MODEL), so callers cannot re-assert it. The previous behavior is not reimplemented anywhere else in the repo.

findings.title: Restore -s read-only sandbox pin removed from codex exec argv
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` (non-interactive, no approval prompts) with cwd=opts.repoPath and an arbitrary prompt on stdin — i.e. an autonomous agent over untrusted repo content, a classic prompt-injection surface. At base (ca2e814:line 20) the agent's tool sandbox was hard-pinned to `read-only`, so every write/mutation by the agent was rejected regardless of local config. This diff deletes `-s read-only` and replaces it with nothing (`rg -n 'sandbox|"-s"' src/` on head returns no pin anywhere in the tree). The sandbox policy now silently inherits the ambient Codex config (~/.codex/config.toml `sandbox` setting / profiles), which on developer and CI machines is frequently `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`. On such hosts the agent can now modify or delete files in the target repo (and with danger-full-access, escape beyond it) where the previous code path rejected every write — a security downgrade and potential data-loss/tamper path introduced solely by this removed flag. There is no compensating control: no `--config sandbox=`, no env pin, no other line in the diff.

findings.title: Removed `-s read-only` sandbox pin on codex exec; sandbox now config-dependent
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 20 previously pinned `codex exec` to `read-only`, an unconditional guarantee independent of host state. With the flag removed, the spawned agent's sandbox_mode is resolved from ambient Codex configuration (`sandbox_mode` / active profile in ~/.codex/config.toml, `--sandbox` defaults). On any host configured with `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `"danger-full-access"`, `spawnSync` (line 23) now runs an AI agent — prompted with untrusted PR-derived content, cwd set to `opts.repoPath` (line 24) — with permission to mutate the host repository or, in danger-full-access, execute arbitrary commands. The reviewed code being able to write to or escape the review environment is exactly what the deleted flag prevented; on default configs the code silently relies on the compiled read-only default instead of enforcing it.

findings.title: Diff base no longer normalized: two-dot diff vs PR_BASE_SHA reviews upstream commits as PR changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line `mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` made the patch three-dot (branch-only) for ANY PR_BASE_SHA value. The env var's namesake, github.event.pull_request.base.sha, is the base branch TIP, not the merge point. Substituting that value with a PR-head checkout: old code diffed merge-base(baseTip, head)..head (exactly the PR's changes, matching GitHub's Files-changed view); new code runs `git diff baseTip..HEAD` (lines 139-140), which includes every commit main made since divergence, shown as reversals/deletions of work the PR author never touched. bundle.patch (line 166) feeds review() (line 176), so verdicts can request changes on clean PRs for 'reverting' main's own commits; changedFiles (line 140 -> changedPaths line 141) now includes upstream-only files, so inlineComments (line 81) can emit comments on files/lines outside the real PR diff -> GitHub rejects the whole review POST with 422 and postReview's catch silently degrades to a body-only review. Additionally the patch now keys on literal 'HEAD' while reviews/checks post against headSha (line 137), so with PR_HEAD_SHA set to a different SHA the posted commit is not the reviewed content. findings.title: Diff base switched from merge-base to PR_BASE_SHA, phantom-reverting main
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code collapsed the diff base to the true common ancestor (`git merge-base baseSha headSha`) before diffing. The new code diffs `baseSha..HEAD` verbatim. When PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip (the standard meaning of a PR's base SHA, e.g. github.event.pull_request.base.sha) and the PR branch is behind main — the normal stale-branch case — merge-base(baseSha, HEAD) != baseSha, so `git diff baseSha HEAD` contains reversed hunks of commits merged to main since the fork and `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` lists files the PR never touched. Substituted with real values in a scratch clone: baseSha=base-tip on a stale branch yields changed files [main.txt, pr.txt] where the old path yields [pr.txt], and the patch includes `-mainline` (phantom deletion of an upstream-only file). This polluted patch/changedFiles flows into the bundle (lines 162-172) and review() (line 176); findings for unrelated files now pass the changedPaths filter (line 63), so the bot posts inline review comments on lines the PR never touched (postReview, line 178) and can post a REQUEST_CHANGES review whose check concludes 'failure' (line 179 + VERDICT_CONCLUSION), failing a clean PR. Second defect in the same hunk: the patch endpoint changed from env-overridden `headSha` to literal "HEAD", while the review/check are still attached to env headSha (commit_id/head_sha, lines 85/124 via calls at 178-179) — if the checked-out HEAD differs from PR_HEAD_SHA (newer push, merge-commit checkout), the reviewed content is not the tree of the commit receiving the verdict.

findings.title: Removed merge-base normalization: PR_BASE_SHA env path now diffs base tip, not fork point
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code computed mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) (old line 139), which normalizes any PR_BASE_SHA to the true fork point, then diffed mergeBase..headSha and listed files from mergeBase. New code runs git diff baseSha HEAD and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) directly. When PR_BASE_SHA is set to the base branch TIP rather than the fork point (the common CI convention, e.g. GitHub's github.event.pull_request.base.sha) and the checkout is the PR head, any commits that landed on the base branch after the fork point now appear in the patch as reverse-diffs and in changedFiles as changed paths. The LLM reviewer then reviews changes the PR never made, and inlineComments() (line 81) only filters findings against changedPaths — which now includes those upstream files — so inline review comments can be posted on lines/files the PR did not touch. The default path (no env) is unaffected: merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) is an ancestor of HEAD, so the removed recompute resolved back to baseSha.

findings.title: String-form replace() reinterprets $ patterns in bundle/patch, corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a STRING replacement argument interprets the special patterns $$ (→$), $& (→matched text), $` (→text before match) and $' (→text after match); a function replacer returns its value verbatim. The base code deliberately used function replacers (verified via git show 0e97403:src/core/review.ts) — the standard idiom to suppress exactly this interpretation. This diff reverts all three sites ({{BUNDLE}} at 23-26, {{FINDINGS}}/{{PATCH}} at 32-33) to string arguments. The injected values are repo-derived review content: JSON.stringify(bundle) embeds the PR diff/file contents and bundle.patch is the raw patch, where $$ (shell/Makefile/CI), $&, $`, $' occur routinely (e.g. a patch line containing $' splices the entire remainder of the prompt template into itself, and $$ collapses to $). The corrupted string is consumed at line 28 (runCodex(reviewPrompt)) and line 34 (runCodex(criticPrompt)), so the model silently reviews mangled input and extractJson can receive prompt text that no longer matches what the author reviewed — a silent corruption of the tool's core input path with no error raised.

findings.title: Fallback review drops commit_id, misattributing verdict to latest commit
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview still takes headSha (line 79) and the primary path pins the review to it via payload commit_id (line 89), but the catch-branch call (lines 101-111) now posts only event and body. Per GitHub's create-review API, omitting commit_id attaches the review to the PR's latest commit at post time. The fallback executes after `await review(bundle)` (line 182), which can run for minutes; if a commit is pushed during that window, or the fallback fires for any other reason where head is ahead, the verdict computed against headSha (pass / REQUEST_CHANGES / findings body) is attributed to a newer, unreviewed commit. A REQUEST_CHANGES then lands on code never reviewed and never becomes 'outdated' relative to the reviewed SHA, while the sibling check run still pins head_sha=headSha (line 128 via caller line 184) — review and check-run point at different commits. The two branches of the same operation now have silently divergent commit-attribution behavior, with no rationale in the (empty) commit message.

findings.title: Fallback review POST drops commit_id, mis-attaching verdict to latest commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The GitHub 'Create a review' API, when commit_id is omitted, places the review on the LATEST commit of the pull request. The primary POST (line 89) still pins commit_id: headSha, but if it fails (typically a 422 from an out-of-range inline comment line), the fallback now posts event+body with no commit pin. The review runs an async LLM review (runGithub line 183), so a push during review is realistic: (1) normal push during review — base pinned the REQUEST_CHANGES/pass verdict to the reviewed SHA; head attaches it to the newer, never-reviewed commit, while postCheck (line 128) simultaneously pins its check-run to the old headSha, producing contradictory PR signals; (2) force-push during review — base's fallback 422'd with the stale sha and the outer catch posted an honest 'review failed' check; head silently posts the stale verdict against the new unreviewed code and it reads as a pass. The invariant this bot exists to enforce (verdict bound to exactly the reviewed commit) is silently broken precisely when the fallback runs. Minimal fix restores the two deleted array entries.

findings.title: normalizeFinding now fabricates defaults for malformed findings instead of rejecting
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (public swallow site). Base behavior: every malformed field threw ('malformed finding: invalid severity/missing file/invalid lineStart'), so normalizeReview (and via it, the whole review pipeline) failed loudly on unusable model output; the old strict=false path preserved distinguishability by DROPPING invalid entries. New behavior silently coerces: severity 'BLOCKER'/garbage/missing → "P1" (a blocking-grade severity) @98; unknown category → "bug" @100-102; missing file → "" @103; lineStart/lineEnd → 0, or NaN when non-numeric (e.g. "abc" → NaN, which serializes to null) @104-105; missing title → "Untitled finding" @99; whyItBreaks/suggestedFix → "" @107-108. Even a non-object element (findings:["garbage"]) — the non-object guard was also deleted — yields a complete fabricated Finding {severity:'P1', category:'bug', file:'', lineStart:0}. This violates the Finding contract itself (a finding must cite a concrete changed file and lineStart ≥ 1): downstream consumers of RawReview (verdict computation reading severity, PR-comment posting reading file/lineStart) receive fabricated findings indistinguishable from real ones, with no log and no error signal anywhere. The removal of the strict parameter @113,131 compounds it: former strict=false callers that relied on invalid findings being filtered out of the array now get them included as fabricated P1/bug entries — same input, materially different output, no signal. Exported API defect: every eventual caller is forced to act on failure-as-value.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently coerces malformed findings into fabricated P1s

findings.title: normalizeFinding now fabricates P1/bug findings from malformed input instead of rejecting

findings.title: Drop -R breaks gh repo resolution in pre-checkout refs step
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step is the first step of the job (line 26); no actions/checkout has run when the else-branch executes (the workflow_dispatch path, since EVENT_HEAD is empty there). `gh pr view` resolves the repository from the git remote of the working directory; at this point GITHUB_WORKSPACE is empty on a fresh/first-run self-hosted runner, so gh fails with 'could not determine the current repository' (GH_TOKEN does not substitute for -R). On a warm runner it works only incidentally, via a leftover .git from the checkout step of a previous run — nondeterministic repo resolution. Worse, the failure is silent: `echo "head=$(gh ...)"` exits 0 even when the substitution fails (pre-existing pattern on these changed lines), so steps.refs.outputs.head/base become empty and the subsequent 'Checkout PR head' step (line 45) checks out the wrong ref and the review runs against wrong/empty SHAs instead of failing loudly. The removed `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}` / `-R "$REPO"` was the deterministic mechanism; nothing compensates for it.

findings.title: Restore -R "$REPO": gh cannot infer repo before checkout; refs silently become empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `-R "$REPO"` (and its `REPO` env) made repo resolution deterministic and cwd-independent. The 'Resolve PR refs' step is the FIRST step of the job — no actions/checkout has run yet (checkout is at line 42) — so in the else branch (reachable only via workflow_dispatch, where EVENT_HEAD is empty) `gh pr view` must infer the repository from git remotes in GITHUB_WORKSPACE. On a fresh/ephemeral self-hosted runner (or after workspace cleanup) the workspace is not a git repo, gh fails with 'could not determine base repo', and because the calls sit inside `echo "head=$(...)"`, the `bash -e` step does NOT fail (exit status of the simple command `echo` is 0) — empty `head`/`base` are written to GITHUB_OUTPUT. `actions/checkout` at line 45 then receives `ref: ''` and falls back to the dispatch ref (default branch, not the PR head), and the review step runs with PR_BASE_SHA=''/PR_HEAD_SHA='' against the wrong checkout: the manual PR-review path is broken, silently.

findings.title: Restore -R repo pin: gh pr view can no longer resolve the repo pre-checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes both `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}` (line 29 of base) and the `-R "$REPO"` flag, leaving `gh pr view` to infer the repository from the `GH_REPO` env (not set; the runner exports GITHUB_REPOSITORY, which gh does not read) or a git remote in the current working directory. This step runs FIRST in the job, before `actions/checkout`, so on a fresh/cleaned self-hosted runner (or any hosted runner) the workspace has no `.git` and `gh` exits non-zero with 'could not determine base repo: no git remotes found'. Concretely: on `workflow_dispatch` (the only path reaching this branch, since pull_request events short-circuit on EVENT_HEAD), the 'Resolve PR refs' step fails, head/base outputs are never produced, and the checkout at lines 42-46 and review step at lines 52-58 never run — the manual review workflow is broken. On a warmed runner whose leftover workspace has an origin pointing elsewhere, the PR number is silently resolved against the wrong repository, yielding wrong head/base SHAs for the review.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-output errors into an empty pass-shaped review
