The head version deletes all five throws and substitutes defaults: raw=null → {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}; findings:"none" (a common model malformation) → [] at line 115-117; summary:123 → "123"/summary:{} → "[object Object]" at line 125; checked/residual_risks non-array → [] at lines 118-123, 127. Callers can no longer distinguish 'output failed validation' from 'legitimate empty review': a malformed result with a plausible summary and a non-array findings field now reads as a zero-finding review. This is a removed error-propagation branch on an exported function taking untrusted `raw: any` — every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value, so the defect is in the shipped contract itself, independent of in-repo callers (none exist in this repo slice).

findings.title: normalizeReview now swallows malformed-review errors as silent empty defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw Error("malformed review output: ...") at base src/shared/schema.ts:115-131 when raw was not an object, or summary/findings/checked/residual_risks were missing or non-array/non-string. The diff deletes all five guards and replaces failure with silent defaults: summary becomes String(raw?.summary ?? "") (head:125), findings become [] (head:115-117), checked become [] (head:127), residual_risks become [] (head:118-123). There is no throw, no log, and no marker, so a garbage payload (e.g. {"error":"rate_limited"}, a truncated model response, or findings as a string) is normalized to summary:"" with zero findings and zero residual risks — indistinguishable from a legitimately clean review. In this module's own contract (Verdict = pass|changes_requested|needs_human, ReviewResult at head:75-83) zero findings + zero blocking residual_risks is exactly the 'pass' shape, so a failed parse can now flow downstream as a clean 'no issues' result instead of aborting. Callers can no longer distinguish 'failed' from a real empty review at any decision point.

findings.title: normalizeReview now swallows malformed-review errors as empty defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version of normalizeReview threw 'malformed review output: ...' for five distinct structural failures: non-object input (old lines 115-117), non-string summary (118-120), and non-array findings/checked/residual_risks (121-131). This diff deletes all five throws and substitutes defaults: summary falls back to String(raw?.summary ?? "") (line 125) and findings/checked/residual_risks fall back to [] (lines 115-117, 127, 118-123). Substitution: normalizeReview(null) previously threw at the caller's catch block, where failure could be retried, logged, or mapped to needs_human; now it returns { summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] } — a structurally valid RawReview indistinguishable from a genuine review that found zero issues and has no blocking residual risks. Per RawReview's sibling types in the same file (Verdict = "pass" | "changes_requested" | "needs_human", line 22), an empty review maps naturally to a pass verdict, so a truncated/corrupted model response gets silently converted into 'review passed with no findings'. As an exported symbol (export function, line 114) with no in-repo caller to distinguish failure from value, the API contract itself forces every eventual caller to treat failure as a real empty review — the swallow site is the present defect.

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer in git(): full git diff now overflows 1 MiB default
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's default 1024*1024 (1 MiB) stdout cap. The primary caller git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at src/adapters/local.ts:100 captures the entire PR patch, whose size is unbounded user content; patches >1 MiB are routine for the PRs this tool reviews. On overflow Node kills the child, sets res.error=ENOBUFS and res.status=null, so line 12 throws `git diff <base> <head> failed: ` with empty stderr — runLocal aborts and no review is produced for large diffs. The sibling gh() at lines 32-37 deliberately keeps maxBuffer:1024*1024*64, confirming the 64 MiB budget was intentional for variable-size command output; git diff is at least as large as gh output. This regresses the tool's core path for exactly the inputs it exists to handle.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git(): diff >1MiB now aborts review with empty error
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (was 64 MiB before this change). git() captures the full PR patch via `git diff baseSha HEAD` (src/adapters/local.ts:100) and file list via `git diff --name-only` (:101); a diff exceeding 1 MiB (lockfiles, vendored/generated code) makes Node kill the git child: res.status becomes null and the cause is stored in res.error, which the code never reads. The `res.status !== 0` check then throws `git diff <base> <head> failed: ` with an empty stderr, so the entire review of a large PR fails with a blank reason. gh() at line 36 retains the identical 64MB buffer, showing the constant is still needed in this codebase and the removal is unintentional.

findings.title: git() lost maxBuffer: diffs >1 MiB now abort the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` makes spawnSync use Node's default maxBuffer of 1,048,576 bytes. The same helper runs `git diff baseSha, HEAD` (src/adapters/local.ts:100) and puts the untruncated output into the review bundle as `patch`. For any PR whose combined diff exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync kills git (res.error = ENOBUFS), res.status is null instead of 0, so the guard at src/adapters/local.ts:12 throws `git diff <base> <head> failed:` with an empty stderr (git never wrote to stderr; the real cause sits unread in res.error). runLocal then rejects and no review is produced — a workflow that succeeded up to 64 MiB before this change. The sibling gh() helper (src/adapters/local.ts:33-37) still carries maxBuffer: 64 MiB, confirming the removal on git() is inconsistent for the same large-output command class.

findings.title: Error-path check conclusion 'failure'→'neutral' downgrades the review-errored signal
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (public gating path, failure mapped to a non-failing value). The 'Needlefish' check run is this adapter's public result contract. Previously an errored review posted conclusion 'failure' (red, previously_reached=src/adapters/github.ts:191 in base c0bd9e30). Now it posts 'neutral', so: (1) severity inverts — VERDICT_CONCLUSION maps changes_requested→'failure' (line 52) and needs_human→'neutral' (line 53), so a crashed review (nothing reviewed, verdict unknown) now reports as a better outcome than a completed review that requested changes, and is indistinguishable from 'needs_human' at the conclusion level; (2) any automation/dashboards branching on the conclusion can no longer distinguish 'review failed' from 'needs_human' — only the title text does; (3) the summary still asserts 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR' (line 193) while the conclusion asserts a neutral, non-failing state. The escape hatch 'still logged' does not hold at the decision point: stderr + process.exitCode=1 (lines 195-196) are host-job signals, not the check-run contract consumers of the 'Needlefish' check read. Note this is signal loss, not a merge bypass: a required status check is only satisfied by 'success', so 'neutral' still blocks.

findings.title: patch (three-dot via gh pr diff) no longer matches changedFileSet (two-dot)
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch is now GitHub's three-dot diff (merge-base→head) from `gh pr diff`, but changedFileSet (line 56) still computes `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` — two-dot — with baseSha = pr.base?.sha, i.e. the current tip of the base branch (line 141). On any PR whose base branch advanced after it branched (the common case for open PRs), changedFiles/changedPaths include files changed only on the base branch, which have no hunks in the patch. The review bundle's changed-file list and surface classification then describe changes that are not part of this PR; before this diff both sides used the same two-dot base so the inputs were consistent.

findings.title: Errored review now posts check conclusion 'neutral', which passes required-check gates
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path in runGithub now posts the Needlefish check run with conclusion 'neutral' instead of 'failure'. GitHub treats 'neutral' check runs as satisfying required status/branch-protection gates (like 'success'/'skipped'), so when review() crashes the PR becomes MERGEABLE with zero review performed — the gate fails open. This contradicts the tool's own verdict mapping, where even a 'changes_requested' verdict (a completed, human-readable review) maps to conclusion 'failure' (VERDICT_CONCLUSION, line ~92): an errored review should block at least as hard. The unchanged summary text still asserts 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.' while the conclusion now semantically passes merge gates, so humans reading the check plus any auto-merge keyed on the required check will treat an unreviewed PR as passable. Previously the crashed review failed the required check and blocked merge.

findings.title: Patch now comes from API merge-base diff but changedFileSet still diffs base-branch tip
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch now comes from `gh pr diff` (server-side merge-base..head — the PR's own changes only), but changedFileSet (line 144, unchanged) still runs local `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` where baseSha = pr.base.sha is the base branch TIP. On any branch behind its base (very common), the local diff additionally lists files changed only on main (as reverse changes), so bundle.changedFiles/changedPaths describe a different diff than the patch given to the reviewer. Two concrete breakages follow: (1) the reviewer, told via bundle.changedFiles that main-only files changed, can emit findings on files absent from the PR diff; inlineComments() passes them (they ARE in changedPaths), the create-review POST is rejected 422 by GitHub (comment path not in the PR diff), and postReview's catch silently re-posts without ANY inline comments (lines 91-108); (2) conversely, a PR file whose final contents match the base tip (e.g. the PR reverts a main change) is in the patch but missing from changedPaths, so its legitimate inline comments are dropped by the changedPaths.has(f.file) filter (line 63). Before this diff, patch and changedFileSet were both the same local `git diff baseSha HEAD`, so the two sets were provably consistent; this change breaks that invariant.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization; 'p0'/'P0 ' now silently becomes P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is the sanitization boundary for untyped external payloads: normalizeReview(raw: any) at src/shared/schema.ts:132 maps raw.findings straight through it, and the field-level String()/Number()/clamp calls show untrusted input is the expected case. The base code recovered case/whitespace variants (String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase(), base line 96) and defaulted unparseable values to the HIGH-visibility "P1". The new code accepts only exact uppercase matches (SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) at src/shared/schema.ts:97) and defaults everything else to the LOWEST severity "P3". Substitution: raw.severity="p0" (or "P0 ") → guard SEVERITIES.includes("p0") @97 → false branch → severity="P3". Base produced "P0". A critical finding is silently downgraded to the lowest priority — indistinguishable at the only consumer (normalizeReview @132) from a genuine P3 — which corrupts triage and any downstream verdict gating that branches on P0/P1 (Trigger D: failure-to-classify now lands as a plausible real value, in the bury-it direction).

findings.title: Removed severity canonicalization silently downgrades case/whitespace variants to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is the sanitization boundary for untyped external review JSON (normalizeReview takes `raw: any` and feeds it in at src/shared/schema.ts:132). The old body did String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES membership test, so "p1", " P1 ", "p0" were recognized as valid severities. The new body tests raw.severity directly, so any non-canonical spelling now fails SEVERITIES.includes and falls back to the default — which this same diff changed from "P1" to "P3". Net effect: a genuine P0/P1 finding whose severity string is lowercase or padded is silently reclassified as P3 (lowest severity, per this schema's own semantics), burying it with no error or signal. This is a regression of defensive handling on the exact input path (untyped `any` JSON) the function exists to normalize; the compound P1→P3 default change makes the misclassification maximally lossy instead of lossy-toward-attention.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization: "p1"/" P0 " now silently become P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is the boundary that canonicalizes untrusted review output (normalizeReview takes raw:any and maps every finding through it at src/shared/schema.ts:132). The old code canonicalized input via String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase(), so "p0", " P1 ", or "p2\n" resolved to the intended Severity; unknown values fell back to P1. The new code runs SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) on the raw value with no case/whitespace/type normalization, so every non-exact variant now misses the membership test and falls back to "P3" — the lowest severity. Since severity drives the blocking verdict downstream, a model-emitted "p0" or "p1" finding is silently reclassified as non-blocking P3, indistinguishable from a genuine P3 (swallowed signal: failure-to-match now maps to the least-urgent value, and the fallback itself was also changed P1→P3, flipping the malformed-input posture from escalate to de-emphasize). This is contract drift on an exported symbol: the name/type promise 'normalize a Partial<Finding> into a canonical Finding' is no longer implemented for the severity field.

findings.title: Restore token-stripping: codex child now inherits GitHub creds via process.env
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the `env` copy that stripped GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN and also drops the `env` option from spawnSync. Node's documented default for `env` is `process.env`, so the spawned `codex exec` agent process now receives the parent's GitHub credentials verbatim. codex runs model-generated commands in the repo; the `-s read-only` flag sandboxing the filesystem does not stop the agent from reading its own environment (e.g. `echo $GITHUB_TOKEN` in any spawned shell) and exfiltrating the token. The base commit deliberately stripped exactly these variables, so this regresses an intentional credential-isolation control on the only path that spawns the agent.

findings.title: Restore secret scrub: spawned codex agent now inherits GitHub tokens
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN, passing the scrubbed env to spawnSync. This diff removes both the scrub and the `env` option, and Node's spawnSync defaults the child environment to process.env when `env` is omitted. The spawned `codex exec` is an autonomous AI agent fed an arbitrary `prompt` (a PR-review prompt embedding attacker-influencable PR/issue text — a prompt-injection surface). Its `-s read-only` sandbox restricts filesystem writes, not environment visibility: the codex process (and anything it launches) can read its own environ and exfiltrate it. Every one of the runner's GitHub credentials is now handed to that subprocess, re-enabling the credential-exposure path the scrub existed to close.

findings.title: Re-exposes GitHub tokens to spawned codex agent by dropping env scrub

This diff deletes the scrub and the `env` option, so Node's spawnSync inherits the parent's full environment (documented Node behavior: omitting `env` passes process.env). The spawned `codex exec` agent runs model-generated shell commands over untrusted repo/prompt content (`prompt` param, opts.repoPath contents); its read-only sandbox restricts writes, not reading its own environment, so an injected instruction can run `printenv GH_TOKEN` and emit the credential in the final message, which this function reads from lastMsg and returns to its caller. A deliberate credential-containment control on a prompt-injection surface is removed with no compensating control.

findings.title: Fork-PR guard removed: untrusted code now runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow triggers on `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened), which also fires for PRs from forks. The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the ONLY control preventing fork PRs from executing on `runs-on: self-hosted` (verified: no other gate, concurrency group, or environment protection exists in the workflow or repo). After this change, a malicious fork PR runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28 — executes attacker-chosen postinstall scripts from the fork's lockfile) and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34 — runs attacker-authored source) on the persistent, non-ephemeral runner, with GH_TOKEN (pull-requests: write, checks: write) exported into the step environment. GitHub's `pull_request` token sandboxing limits the token, not code execution on the runner machine: the runner's credentials, registration state, and all subsequent jobs on that host are exposed to persistence/poisoning attacks. Escalates to P0 if this repo is public, since any outsider can open a fork PR with zero interaction.

findings.title: Restore anti-fork guard: fork PRs now execute on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` (base afba483, line 19) was the only control restricting the review job to same-repo PRs. For `pull_request` events from forks, GitHub runs the BASE repo's workflow file, so this deletion alone enables fork PRs to trigger the job. Same-repo PRs always passed the equality check, so the ONLY behavior this change adds is fork execution. On a fork PR the job now: (1) runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18) — a persistent machine, not an ephemeral GitHub-hosted VM; (2) checks out attacker-controlled PR head code with `actions/checkout@v4 ref: pull_request.head.sha` (lines 20-24); (3) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) where the attacker controls both package.json and the committed lockfile, so malicious postinstall scripts execute; (4) runs `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) — arbitrary attacker code. Result: untrusted fork code executes on the self-hosted host (runner credentials file `~/.actions-runner/.credentials`, host secrets/caches, persistence, network position are all exposed). The default read-only GITHUB_TOKEN on fork PRs does not mitigate host-level compromise. This `if` guard is exactly the control GitHub's security-hardening docs prescribe for `pull_request` workflows on self-hosted runners; there is no compensating in-repo mitigation (no environment protection rules, no workflow_run pattern — the repo contains only this workflow).

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard: self-hosted job now executes untrusted fork PR code

The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18), checks out the PR head (line 20-23), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) — which executes the root project's preinstall/postinstall/prepare scripts from the untrusted PR checkout (pnpm's dependency build-script blocking does not apply to the root project, and the PR can also edit package.json to allowlist dependency build scripts) — and then directly executes the PR's own source via `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34); the workflow's own header comment states the PR checkout's src/ IS the executed tool. The job also carries `pull-requests: write` + `checks: write` permissions and GH_TOKEN, which fork PRs receive for PR/checks scopes. The deleted guard existed precisely to fence this; its removal is a security bypass on the supply-chain surface, not a style change.

findings.title: Explicit 0ms env durations silently fall back to defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs feeds NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (line 3, fallback 5000) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (line 7, fallback 2000), both used as setTimeout delays in the timeout kill chain (lines 123-124). Unset/empty input is already handled at line 133, so under `parsed >= 0` an explicit `0` was the only way to configure 'SIGKILL immediately after timeout' or 'stop waiting immediately after SIGKILL' — and it worked: setTimeout(…, 0) is valid (Node clamps to 1ms) and finish() clears the timers via the settled guard. After this change `0 > 0` is false, so an operator who sets either env var to 0 gets 5000/2000ms instead, with no warning: the configured kill timing silently changes on an operator-facing config surface and the 0ms configuration becomes inexpressible. Substitution performed: value=0 → line 135 branch taken → fallbackMs returned → setTimeout at line 124 (grace) / line 123 (give-up) receive 5000/2000 instead of the configured 0.

findings.title: Large-PR review silently skips changed files not mapped to top-6 hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Base appended a tail-coverage hotspot for any changed file not covered by the selected hotspots (base lines 98-110, invariant: 'never silently skip a changed file'). Head keeps only slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS=6), so on any large PR where the LLM map emits >6 hotspots or omits files, the uncovered files get no deep review and nothing in the output (checked, residual_risks, summary) reports the gap — the delivered review claims coverage it does not have.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks hard-coded to [] before critic, dropping block signals
findings.whyItBreaks: Base pushed res.residual_risks from every hotspot (base:127) into candidateMerged.residual_risks (base:140), so the critic saw each deep pass's verification gaps and blocks:true flags. Head discards res.residual_risks in the loop (only findings/summary are read, lines 103-105) and hardcodes residual_risks: [] (line 113). The critic prompt (line 116) therefore contains an empty list, and deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) at line 122 can only see residuals the critic invents on its own — a hotspot that reported 'could not verify X, blocks:true' now cannot influence the verdict or the returned residualRisks (line 128). Failure/warning signals are conflated with 'no risks'.

findings.title: Per-hotspot fault isolation removed: one deep-pass failure aborts whole large review

Head removes the catch: any single transient LLM/parse failure in one of up to 6 sequential deep passes throws out of reviewLarge, discarding all completed hotspots' findings and producing no ReviewResult at all. The failure is loud (not silent), but the pipeline went from graceful degradation to all-or-nothing on a path with 6 sequential network-dependent calls.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks hard-dropped in large reviews (residual_risks: [])
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code pushed every deep pass's res.residual_risks (including blocks:true 'unverified hotspot / deep pass failed' signals) into candidateMerged.residual_risks, which reached the critic via the {{FINDINGS}} prompt and from there the final residualRisks and deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks). New code stops collecting res.residual_risks entirely (line 103) and hardcodes residual_risks: [] (line 113), so a deep reviewer's blocked/unverified-surface signal can structurally never reach the critic input, the returned residualRisks, or the verdict — while the small-PR path still forwards candidate.residual_risks (line 60), confirming this is a large-path regression, not a redesign. A large PR whose deep passes flagged unverifiable hotspots can now return a clean result with no trace. TRIGGER D: signal mapped to empty value; at review.ts:122 and the return's residualRisks the absence of residuals is indistinguishable from 'nothing was flagged'.

findings.title: Large reviews silently skip changed files beyond the 6-hotspot cap

Whenever the map pass emits more than 6 hotspots (files of hotspots 7+ are sliced away) or the LLM under-assigns files, those changed files now receive zero deep review and nothing records the gap — no checked entry, no residual, no finding. Large mode is exactly the >30k-char / >10-file case, so the riskiest PRs can get a 'completed' review that silently never looked at part of the diff. The removed catch-block also means the loop at 97-106 now aborts the whole review on the first deep-pass failure instead of recording and continuing — fail-loud, but it destroys all completed hotspot work on one flaky LLM response.

findings.title: Tail-coverage backstop removed: uncovered changed files silently skip deep review

Coverage could be lost two ways that both still exist: `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93) deterministically drops hotspots 7+ including their files when the LLM map pass returns more than 6, and the LLM map can simply omit files. Now those files are never deep-reviewed, and since candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded [] (line 113), no signal of the gap reaches the critic or the final result — the returned review silently claims coverage it does not have. The critic cannot compensate: it only receives patchStat (line 117), not the diff or the file list.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks silently discarded before critic and verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: Base line 127 did `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` and fed them into candidateMerged.residual_risks, so deep-pass residuals (the schema's channel for blocking, non-finding risk signals) reached the critic FINDINGS JSON and could flow into pruned.residual_risks. Consequently deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) at line 122 and the returned residualRisks (line ~126) can never contain a deep-origin residual: a deep pass reporting blocks:true risk now behaves identically to one reporting none, so the verdict can flip from BLOCK to APPROVE while unresolved risk exists. Failure/risk signal is conflated with 'no risk'.

findings.title: Removing per-hotspot try/catch lets one deep-pass failure abort the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: Base lines 123-132 caught a failing deep pass, recorded '[name] DEEP PASS FAILED' in checked plus a blocks:true residual, and continued with the remaining hotspots — the review still completed with an explicit signal of what was not reviewed. The change makes the throw propagate out of reviewLarge, so one transient failure (malformed LLM output — a failure mode the code itself guards against at lines 57 and 120, or a runCodex error) on any of up to 6 deep passes destroys the entire large-PR review after the map pass and any successful deep passes have already run; the caller gets no review at all instead of a degraded, correctly-flagged one.

findings.title: Large-PR path silently drops focus/deep inputs; {{FOCUS}} placeholder left unsubstituted

findings.title: Focus/deep removed only from large-PR path; hints silently dropped there

findings.whyItBreaks: The Bundle type is unchanged by this PR (patchStat: only src/core/review.ts changed), so `focus` and `deep` remain first-class inputs the runner still populates (the bundle format carries both fields). findings.title: formatDuration can emit "Nm 60s" when remainder rounds to 60
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) without carrying into minutes. For any ms where minutes > 0 and (ms % 60000) is in [59500, 59999] — e.g. ms=119500 — seconds rounds to 60 and the function returns "1m 60s"; the old code (round total seconds first, then split) returned "2m 0s" for the same input. This output flows verbatim into the user-facing markdown stats line at render.ts:75 (per-step durations) and render.ts:80 ("total N"), so review summaries can contain "… 1m 60s → … · total 1m 60s", which is never a valid duration rendering. Verified by substitution: ms=119500 → old "2m 0s", new "1m 60s"; ms=119999 → old "2m 0s", new "1m 60s".
